query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an fcc matrix, elevated-temperature exposure in oxidizing environments leads to selective oxidation of the more reactive alloying elements (particularly Cr and Ti) along grain boundaries. This oxidation yields a nonuniform, poorly adherent oxide network that depletes key strengthening elements locally, thereby creating embrittled intergranular regions that serve as crack initiation sites and can ultimately trigger catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built HEA in a single-phase, fcc state with a relatively uniform elemental distribution and minimal pre-existing oxide scales.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to elevated temperatures (700–900°C) under controlled gas atmospheres with systematically varied oxygen partial pressures (from oxidizing to reducing conditions).
generation.conditions: Temperature range from 700°C to 900°C with exposures up to 48 hours in controlled atmospheres; comparisons between oxidizing (high oxygen partial pressure) and reducing/inert conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of selectively oxidized grain-boundary regions (mainly Cr-oxide and Ti-oxide phases) that locally deplete the alloy of these elements, leading to weakened, embrittled interfaces.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, oxygen diffuses preferentially along grain boundaries. The reactive Cr and Ti oxidize to form a heterogeneous oxide scale that does not adhere well to the underlying matrix. Spallation or cracking of this scale leads to localized depletion of these elements, reducing cohesion and mechanical strength at the grain boundaries, thereby facilitating intergranular crack initiation and rapid propagation under mechanical load.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, the HEA will exhibit thicker and more inhomogeneous oxide layers along grain boundaries, increased micro-cracking, and reduced ductility/strength compared to samples in reducing atmospheres. In contrast, reducing conditions should minimize oxide formation and delay or prevent catastrophic failure.
generation.baseline: Untreated, as-manufactured HEA samples tested at room temperature without significant oxidation or microstructural degradation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for exposures at temperatures between 700°C and 900°C over time periods up to 48 hours. Beyond these conditions (e.g., much lower temperatures or extremely long exposures), additional degradation mechanisms might become significant.
generation.uncertainty: There remains some uncertainty regarding the relative oxidation kinetics of Cr versus Ti, and whether other transient phases or diffusion processes might compete with or modify the predicted oxidation-driven embrittlement. The precise contribution of each oxide to mechanical degradation is not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical HEA samples and subject them to elevated temperature (700°C and 900°C) tests under controlled oxidizing (e.g., air or high oxygen partial pressure) versus reducing/inert atmospheres. After exposure, characterize the oxide scale thickness, composition, and distribution along grain boundaries using electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) coupled with EDS, and perform mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness and tensile tests) to assess embrittlement and crack propagation behavior.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via SEM/TEM imaging)
Elemental distribution along grain boundaries (via EDS or atom probe tomography)
Mechanical properties such as tensile strength, ductility, and fracture toughness
Crack density or micro-crack length distribution in oxidized regions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples exposed under oxidizing conditions do not display significantly more pronounced grain-boundary oxidation, depletion of reactive elements, or a corresponding reduction in mechanical integrity (compared to those in reducing/inert conditions), then the role of selective oxidation as the governing degradation mechanism would be refuted.

cited_evidence.text:
High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe oxidation behavior of an equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co high-entropy alloy (HEA) processed by 3D laser printing was investigated at 700 °C and 900 °C. The oxidation kinetics of the alloy followed the parabolic rate law, and the oxidation rate constant increased with the rising of the temperature. Inward diffusion of oxygen and outward diffusion of cations took place during the high-temperature oxidation process. A spinel-type oxide was formed on the surface, and the thickness of the oxide layer increased with the rising of experimental temperature or time. The exfoliation of the oxide layer took place when the test was operated at 900 °C over 12 h. During oxidation tests, the matrix was propped open by oxides and was segmented into small pieces. The formation of loose structures had great effects on the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the HEA.Keywords: metals and alloys, 3D printing, oxidation
